title: The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus
subject: litterature
description: Camus starts from suicide in order to define the absurd. Sisyphus, condemned to roll a rock forever, becomes the hero of a clear-eyed joy.

hero.hook: There is only one truly serious philosophical problem, Camus writes. Then he answers it in the last way you expect.

blocks.text: **The Myth of Sisyphus**, published in **1942**, is where **Albert Camus** founded his thinking on the absurd. Written in the middle of the **Second World War**, it asks how to live without comforting illusions: no religious faith, no political utopias.

Camus leans on **Sisyphus**, the king of Corinth condemned by the gods to useless, endless work, to turn despair into an ethic of freedom. The essay stands beside the novel **The Stranger** in the cycle of the absurd.

sections.title: The divorce between man and the world

blocks.text: Camus opens with a famous line: “There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.” Judging whether life is worth living is the fundamental question. Every thought about meaning starts there.

blocks.caption: Camus in the 1940s: clear sight in the face of the absurd

blocks.text: Camus planned an appendix on Kafka, which the censors cut. He nearly called the manuscript “The Absurd.”

The absurd is not in the world, and not in man alone, but in the meeting of the two. The mind wants order and meaning, and the world stays silent. Recognizing the absurd is the first step toward intellectual honesty, before any answer at all. Camus refuses the false exits, whether they come from religion or from politics.

Camus names three responses to the absurd. Physical suicide removes the one witness of the absurd, which makes it a logical mistake and an escape. Philosophical suicide, the **[[philosophical "leap" (Kierkegaard)]]**, takes shelter in faith or in the irrational and runs from the problem instead of facing it.

The only honest answer is the **[[absurd revolt]]**: standing upright before the silence of the world, holding the tension with no consolation. The absurd man lives in the present, with no metaphysical hope placed in an afterlife or in an end of history.

In Greek mythology, **Sisyphus** cheated death. His punishment: to roll a rock to the top of a mountain forever, and to watch it roll back down every time. Camus is interested in the walk back down. In that moment Sisyphus stands above his fate, because he knows what it is.

blocks.caption: Sisyphus and his rock: useless effort turned into an inner victory

blocks.attribution: Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus

blocks.text: This happiness is not naive. It is the victory of a man who knows his labor will never end, and who takes the struggle itself as enough to fill a heart. Happiness and the absurd are born of the same earth. Camus refuses despair exactly as he refuses illusion.

The essay offers an alternative to the existentialism of **Jean-Paul Sartre**, a philosophy built on freedom and responsibility. Camus proposes instead a freedom that celebrates the present moment. He shaped the **[[Theatre of the Absurd]]** of **Samuel Beckett** and **Eugène Ionesco**, where characters circle in place and never find meaning.

blocks.text: Camus does not deny pain. He refuses to turn it into a doctrine. Sisyphus walks back down the slope knowing exactly what he is doing, and that is what makes a fate livable, at least sometimes. The essay remains an essential companion to **The Stranger**. It also reads the writers of the absurd, from **Dostoevsky** to **Kafka**, to show how art expresses the human condition.
**The Myth of Sisyphus**, published in **1942**, turns the absurd into the **[[absurd revolt]]**: stay lucid, refuse illusions, and imagine Sisyphus happy in his endless struggle.
